newsitem.title: USA: Hilton to formalize ITT offer by week's end.
newsitem.headline: Hilton to formalize ITT offer by week's end.

text.p: Hilton Hotels Corp. said Wednesday it planned to formalise its $6.5 billion hostile bid for ITT Corp. by the end of the week, setting the stage for a battle for control of the owner of Sheraton hotels and Caesars World casinos.

Marc Grossman, senior vice president of corporate affairs, said Hilton will file the documents with the Securities and Exchange Commission which will outline its $55 per share offer for ITT, which also owns various entertainment properties.
Hilton, the nation's largest hotel and gambling company, announced the surprise offer on Monday. By filing the papers with the SEC, Hilton puts pressure on ITT to respond.
As of Wednesday, Grossman said Beverly Hills, Calif.-based Hilton had still not heard from ITT.

Jim Gallagher, a spokesman for New York-based ITT, said the company's board of directors was expected to discuss the offer during its regularly scheduled meeting Feb. 4. He declined to say when a decision would be made.
"Our management has already begun to provide (the board) with the kind of information they'll need in order to make a careful and deliberate examination of the offer," he said.

Previously ITT said within 10 days it would recommend to shareholders whether to accept or reject Hilton's bid, which calls for one-half of the $55 per share price to be paid in cash and one-half in Hilton stock. Hilton also would assume about $4 billion in debt.

Hilton's proposed acquisition is shaping up as a battle with Hilton firing the first legal shot by seeking a court order that would prevent ITT from increasing the size of its board or interfering with the board's election process.

In a lawsuit filed in federal court in Nevada, Hilton said ITT rejected a previous overture from Hilton last November. Because of ITT's disinterest in a merger, Hilton said it was preparing a proxy battle for control of ITT's board.
The suit also seeks to establish Nevada jurisdiction in the matter and prevent ITT from moving any further legal action to other courts in the United States.

"The thrust of Hilton's complaint is that Nevada corporate law bars ITT from precluding its shareholders from exercising their right to accept Hilton's tender offer if they so desire," the company said in court papers. "Accordingly the interpretation of Nevada corporate law will play an essential role in resolution of this matter."
Finally, Hilton is seeking to dismantle ITT's so-called "poison pill," a defensive tactic that, when used, significantly dilutes company ownership and makes an acquisition more expensive.

Late Wednesday, Hilton said the Nevada court set a March 5 hearing date on Hilton's request for an injunction against ITT increasing the size of its board or interfering with the board's election process.

The court, however, denied Hilton's application to prevent ITT from filing suits against Hilton in another court. If ITT does file a lawsuit in another jurisdiction, Hilton can re-apply for an injunction, the court said.

Financial analysts have called Hilton's offer too low, and the prevailing opinion seems to be Hilton will have to raise its bid to somewhere between the mid-60's to the $70 per share level to sucessfully win control of ITT.
If completed, the deal would create the largest lodging and gambling company in the world with 30 casinos and 230,000 hotels rooms.
ITT shares ended trading on Wednesday up 75 cents a share at $57.50. Hilton also traded up on the day, $1.25 to close at $28.875.
